```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(cito)
library(citoMove)
```

## Motivation

The purpose of this appendix is to validate the CNN-SSF model's ability to recover an unknown non-parametric selection rule directly from image input.

In order to isolate the validation from any confounding, I constructed a minimal, controlled binary selection task without any further habitat covariates and without a movement kernel. At each step, the model is shown a choice set of images, mirroring the typical step-selection framework. For each choice set one image is chosen by one defined property of the images. The images show randomly rendered ellipses of varying *roundness*, defined as the proportion of the shortest axis *b* of the ellipses to the longest axis *a*. During rendering the roundest ellipse of each choice set is chosen mathematically, while the CNN-models later task is to chose the roundest ellipse visually. A reliable recovery of the selection rule out of a graphical image feature, would consequently validate the functionality of the function.

## Simulating a controlled binary-choice task

For each of `n_steps` strata, we draw `n_control + 1` candidate ellipses. Each ellipse's *roundness* (ratio of shortest to longest axis) is drawn randomly; the candidate with the highest roundness is chosen (`case_ = TRUE`), analogous to the observed step in a step-selection framework.

```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(100)

nControl <- 9L          
strataSize <- nControl + 1L
nStepsFit <- 50L
nStepsVal <- 50L

simulateRoundnessSteps <- function(step_id, n_per_step = strataSize,
                                    b_min = 1, b_max = 4, a = 4) {
  b_vals    <- runif(n_per_step, min = b_min, max = b_max)
  roundness <- b_vals / a
  case_     <- roundness == max(roundness)

  data.frame(step_id_ = step_id, case_ = case_,
             b_vals = b_vals, roundness = roundness)
}

fit_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nStepsFit), simulateRoundnessSteps))
val_data <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nStepsVal), simulateRoundnessSteps))
```

## Converting ellipses to image arrays

Each ellipse is rendered as a binary image array with a randomly rotated major axis, so the model is forced to learn the shape (roundness) without an influence of the position.

```{r ellipse-image-function}
imgSize <- 250
aMax          <- imgSize / 2 - 10
areaTarget    <- aMax^2 * 0.25

makeEllipseImage <- function(roundness, theta, size = imgSize, area_target = areaTarget) {
  a <- sqrt(area_target / roundness)
  b <- a * roundness

  coords <- seq_len(size) - (size + 1) / 2
  grid    <- expand.grid(x = coords, y = coords)

  x_rot <-  cos(theta) * grid$x + sin(theta) * grid$y
  y_rot <- -sin(theta) * grid$x + cos(theta) * grid$y

  inside <- (x_rot / a)^2 + (y_rot / b)^2 <= 1
  matrix(as.numeric(inside), nrow = size, ncol = size)
}

buildImageArray <- function(data, size = imgSize, seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)
  n      <- nrow(data)
  thetas <- runif(n, min = 0, max = pi)  
  X <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(n, 1, size, size))
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    X[i, 1, , ] <- makeEllipseImage(roundness = data$roundness[i], theta = thetas[i])
  }
  X
}

X     <- buildImageArray(fit_data, seed = 1)
X_val <- buildImageArray(val_data, seed = 2)
```

### Visual check

```{r plot-example-images, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.5}
exampleRows <- which(fit_data$step_id_ == fit_data$step_id_[1])

par(mfrow = c(2, 5), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (i in exampleRows) {
  image(X[i, 1, , ], col = grey.colors(2), axes = FALSE,
        main = paste0("case_=", fit_data$case_[i],
                       "\nround=", round(fit_data$roundness[i], 2)))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## Fitting the CNN-SSF model

The model's architecture is deliberately kept simple with only one convolutional layer to show its ability to efficiently pick up elementary patterns. The architecture's complexity can consequently be scaled up with the complexity of the task. When setting up the architecture I had to adress one further problem specific to the 'relu' activation function: 

```{r fit-model}
Y <- as.numeric(fit_data$case_)

architecture <- create_architecture(conv(n_kernels = 8L, kernel_size = c(3, 3)),
                                     linear(20, activation = "relu"))

m <- cnn_ssf(X = X, Y = Y, density = rep(1, nrow(fit_data)),
             n_control = nControl, architecture = architecture,
             lr = 0.01, epochs = 25)
```

## Validation on independent data

```{r validate}
Y_val <- as.numeric(val_data$case_)

evaluateAccuracy <- function(model, X_new, data_new) {
  pred_raw <- as.vector(predict(model, newdata = X_new))

  df <- data.frame(step_id_ = data_new$step_id_, pred = pred_raw,
                    case_ = data_new$case_)

  softmax <- function(x) exp(x) / sum(exp(x))
  df$prob <- ave(df$pred, df$step_id_, FUN = softmax)

  perStepHit <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(df)), df$step_id_, function(idx) {
    which.max(df$prob[idx]) == which(df$case_[idx])
  })

  list(accuracy = mean(perStepHit), df = df)
}

result <- evaluateAccuracy(m, X_val, val_data)
result$accuracy
```

## Testing model robustness by repeating validation draws

To get an estimate of the model's true recovery rate, I repeat the validation several times on multiple sets of simulated data and analyzing the distribution of accuracies.

```{r repeated-validation}
runValidation <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  val_i   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nStepsVal), simulateRoundnessSteps))
  X_val_i <- buildImageArray(val_i, seed = seed + 1000)
  evaluateAccuracy(m, X_val_i, val_i)$accuracy
}

accs <- sapply(101:110, runValidation)   # 10 different validation data sets
c(mean = mean(accs), sd = sd(accs), min = min(accs), max = max(accs))
```

## Accuracy as a function of task difficulty

In order to test if the remaining error rate is the result of an error in the models or is explainable with the task setup, I checked for one possible task depending explanation. As the visual difference between candidates in choice sets in which the most round candidates are very close can be minimal or, depending on the resolution of the image, even nonexistent, the choice can result in a draw, in which case the model chooses one candidate randomly. To check for this, I test if the model's errors concentrate at these close cases by plotting the differences between the roundness of the two closest candidates of each choice set and analyzing the distribution of the incorrectly chosen instances. A concentration of errors at very close roundness differences hints strongly at this explanation.

```{r difficulty-analysis, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
df <- result$df
df$roundness <- val_data$roundness

margin <- tapply(df$roundness, df$step_id_, function(r) {
  sr <- sort(r, decreasing = TRUE)
  sr[1] - sr[2]              # gap between best and second-best candidate
})

hit <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(df)), df$step_id_, function(idx) {
  which.max(df$prob[idx]) == which(df$case_[idx])
})

plot(margin, as.numeric(hit), pch = 16, col = "grey40",
     xlab = "Roundness margin (best - second-best)", ylab = "Correctly identified (0/1)",
     main = "Prediction accuracy vs. task difficulty")
lo <- lowess(margin, as.numeric(hit))

```

## Testing model learning stability by repeating model fitting and validation

To test the stability of the model training process, I fit the model 5 times on the same simulated data and analyze the validation outcomes.

```{r fit-model}
fitAccuracies <- numeric(10)

for (i in 1:10) {
  
m_i <- cnn_ssf(X = X, Y = Y, density = rep(1, nrow(fit_data)),
             n_control = nControl, architecture = architecture,
             lr = 0.01, epochs = 25)

fitAccuracies[i] <- evaluateAccuracy(m_i, X_val, val_data)$accuracy
}

fitAccuracies
```


## Ablation test to rule out pixel sum shortcut

To rule out the possibility that the model solves the task using the shortcut of summing up pixel intensities rather than learning spatial shape, I do an ablation test in which the pixels of each validation image are randomly shuffled. This preserves the exact number of pixels of the ellipse's area per image while completely destroying its spatial layout.

```{r ablation-shuffle}
n    <- dim(X_val)[1]
size <- dim(X_val)[3]

X_val_shuffled <- array(NA_real_, dim = dim(X_val))
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  X_val_shuffled[i, 1, , ] <- matrix(sample(X_val[i, 1, , ]), nrow = size, ncol = size)
}

result_shuffled <- evaluateAccuracy(m, X_val_shuffled, val_data)
result_shuffled$accuracy
```


## Discussion

**Model robustnes and stability** The CNN-SSF function was able to correctly identify the roundest candidate in averagely 90% of choice sets, with a standard deviation of only 5% between 10 different validation data sets. This result far exceeds the 10% baseline expected if randomly guessed, while the low standard deviation indicates a stable recovery rate. The repeatedly successful learning process indicates a stable fitting process while the ablation test rules out a pixel count shortcut. Destroying the spatial layout of the images dropped the accuracy from around 90 % to the 10 % baseline, which is expected when randomly choosing one candidate out of 10. This proves that the model selection is based on the spatial features of the images.

**Model error analysis** All instances of model error in choosing the roundest candidate occurred at tiny roundness margins below approximately 3%, while all choices in choice sets with larger roundness margins between the top candidates were chosen correctly. This concentration of the models errors on nearly tied candidates hints at the expectable explanation of the model struggling to discriminate ellipses whose axis ratios differ only marginally. This suggests the origin of the remaining error to lie in the task setup rather than a systematical failure of the model to extract graphical features.

**Conclusion** After deliberately isolating the selection choice depending on a single controlled graphical feature, the CNN-SSF function creates a model which is able to reliably recover the graphical choice criteria correctly. This demonstrates that graphical features are correctly captured through the convolutional layers, even with the basic architecture used here, validating the general functionality of the functions approach. To test the approaches usability on real world data, a case study will later be conducted (see Appendix B).
